chunks.text: Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026 CC.No.16046/2018 KABC030436282018 Presented on : 14-06-2018 Registered on : 14-06-2018 Decided on : 22-04-2026 Duration : 7 years, 10 months, 8 days IN THE COURT OF THE XVI ADDITIONAL CHIEF JUDICIAL MAGISTRATE, BENGALURU CITY Dated: This the 22nd day of April 2026 Present: Smt.Tejaswini K.M., B.A.L.LL.M, XVI Addl.C.J.M., Bengaluru City. CC. No.16046/2018 Sri.Anekal Krishnappa S/o Kuppaiah R/at No.111, "Mathru Sri. Nilaya", Girija Shankar Layout, Anekal Taluk, Bangalore Rural District. ....Complainant (By Sri N.M.H., Advocate) Versus 2 C.C..16046/2018 Sri.Srinivasa S/o Bettappa @ Bettaiah R/at No.187/17, Samrudi Nilaya, Behind Shaneshwaa Swamy Temple, Maruthinagara, Sonnenahalli, Bangalore South Taluk, Bangalore - 560068. Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026 .... Accused (By Sri.U.J.H, Advocate) Offence complained : U/Sec.138 of Negotiable Instrument Act. Date of commencement of evidence : 05.06.2018 Date of closing evidence : 06.08.2025 Opinion of the Judge : Accused found guilty Offence complained : U/Sec.138 of Negotiable Instrument Act. Opinion of the Judge : Accused found guilty 3 C.C..16046/2018 JUDGMENT This case is registered against the accused for the offence punishable U/s 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act.

Factual matrix of the complainant's case is as under: It is stated that the accused is the owner of the property bearing site No.187, 1st Stage, formed in Sy.No.17, situated at Sonnenahalli Village, kengeri Hobli within the limits of Sulikere Gramapanchayath, Bangalore South Taluk, measuring East to West 30 feet and North to South 20 feet along with building constructed in ground floor, 1st floor and 2nd floor, the accused has acquired the said property through a Registered Sale Deed dated 26.10.2017. The accused has offered to sell the said property and the offer was accepted by the complainant and accordingly on

2014 the complainant and the accused are entered into an agreement of sale in respect of the said property, total sale consideration was fixed at Rs.11,00,000/-. Accordingly, the complainant has paid a sum of Rs.10,00,000/- through cheque bearing No.413896 drawn on COSMOS Bank, Basavanagudi Branch, Bengaluru to the accused and the accused assured that there is no encumbrance on the said property. The balance consideration amount of Rs.1,00,000/- is to be paid to the accused at the time of registration of the sale deed. But accused unable to comply with the terms and conditions of the agreement of sale and the accused requested the complainant to enter into fresh agreement of sale. Accordingly, on 09.10.2015 the complainant entered into an agreement of sale with the accused. As per the Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026 agreement of sale dated 09.10.2015, the total sale consideration amount was enhanced to Rs.36,00,000/- and the complainant has paid Rs.20,00,000/- in following manner: a) Rs.10,00,000/- by way of cheque bearing No.329275, drawn on Tumkur Grain Merchant Co-operative Bank Ltd. b) Rs.10,00,000/- by way of cash. The complainant has paid total sum of Rs.30,00,000/- to the accused towards part sale consideration amount in pursuance of the agreement of sale dated 07.05.2014 and 09.10.2015. As per the agreement of sale the accused has required to execute and register the sale deed in favour of the complainant within 12 months. But accused postponing in executing the registered sale deed. On repeated requests made by the complainant, towards refund of advance sale consideration, the accused has issued 2 cheques bearing No.465282 dated 06.04.2018 for Rs.30,00,000/- and cheque bearing No.465283 dated 06.04.2018 for Rs.15,86,000/-, drawn on Sri Sudha Co- operative Bank Ltd., Kengeri Branch, Bengaluru. The complainant presented the cheques before the bank, they got dishonoured for the reason 'funds insufficient' vide memos dated 07.04.2018. Therefore, the complainant got issued legal notice on 20.04.2018 demanding the accused to make payment amount within 15 days and it was returned with a shara 'door locked, hence returned to the sender'. However, the accused has not paid the cheques amount. Hence the complainant has constrained to file the present complaint.

After receiving the complaint, this court has meticulously gone through the documents and affidavit filed along with it and then took cognizance of the offence punishable U/sec.138 of Negotiable Instruments Act and ordered for registration of the compliant as P.C.R. Sworn statement of the complainant was recorded and marked 19 documents as Ex.P-1 to P-19. As there were sufficient materials to constitute the offence, this court has proceeded to pass an order for issuing process against the accused. In pursuance of summons, accused has appeared through his counsel and applied for bail. He was enlarged on bail. Then the substance of accusation was read over to the accused in the language known to him, for which he pleaded not guilty. As per the direction of Hon'ble supreme court in "Indian Bank Association V/s Union of India and others reported in (2014)(5) SCC 590, this court treated the sworn statement of the complainant as complainant evidence and posted matter for cross-examination of PW.1. The counsel for the accused has fully cross- examined PW.1. Thereafter the complainant closed his side of evidence. The statement of accused as contemplated under the provisions of Section 313 of Cr.P.C has been recorded vide order dated 06.11.2023 and the incriminating evidence as such forthcoming against the accused in the evidence of PW.1 and the documents has been read over and explained to the Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026 accused in the language known to him. He denied all incriminating evidence. In order to substantiate his defense, the accused got himself examined orally as DW.1 and got marked Ex.D1 to 6. DW.1 has been cross-examined by the learned counsel for the complainant.

I have heard the arguments of the learned counsel for both the side. The learned counsel for complainant filed written arguments. Learned Counsel for both side also filed memo with citations. I have perused the oral and the documentary evidence placed on record and gone through those case laws. Points that arise for my consideration are as under: Whether the complainant proves that the accused towards discharge of his liability issued 2 cheques bearing No.465282 dated 06.04.2018 for Rs.30,00,000/- and cheque bearing No.465283 dated 06.04.2018 for Rs.15,86,000/-, drawn on Sri.Sudha Co- opearative Bank Ltd., Kengeri Branch, Bangalore in favour of complainant, on presentation of the same for encashment, they were dishonored for "Funds Insufficient" in the account maintained by the accused, then in-spite of issuing demand notice to the Accused and in complying with statutory requirement under Negotiable Instrument Act, Accused did not repay the cheques amount, thereby he has committed an offence punishable U/s 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act? What Order? My Answer to above points are as under:- Point No.I :- In the Affirmative, Point No.II :- As per the final order for the following.... REASONS

POINT NO.I:- The Defense of the accused that: He has borrowed Rs.10 lakhs from the complainant through one Mr.Muniyappa, who is manager of Sudha Co- operative Bank. While taking the loan the complainant has put condition to repay the said loan by way of cash and for security purpose he has taken blank e-stamp papers, 10 to 15 blank bond papers and 2 signed cheques and his property documents. He has repaid said loan with interest to the complainant. Thereafter, he requested the complainant to return back his security cheques, but the complainant insisted for higher rate of interest. That time he met Mr.Muniyappa and told him about the same, Mr.Muniyappa assured to get back the documents from the complainant, but in meanwhile Mr.Muniyappa has been murdered and the wife of the Mr.Muniyappa has given complaint against the complainant alleging that he has Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026 murdered him. He has lodged a police compliant against accused. The complainant has misused his security cheques and filed this case. He has not filled the details in the cheques. The complainant has filed several cheque bounce cases against different persons. Hence, on these grounds, accused prays to acquit him from this case.

Advocate for accused has relied on the citations reported CDJ 2024 All HC 180 in between Archana Singh Gautam V/s State of U.P and another, CDJ 2024 APHC 1172 in between Ganta Kavitha Devi V/s The State of Andhra Pradesh, CDJ 2006 SC 492 in between M.S.Narayana Memon @ Mani V/s State of Kerala & Another, CDJ 2001 SC1423 in between Sasseriyil Joseph V/s Devassia, CDJ 2019 SC 471 in between Basalingappa V/s Mudibasappa, CDJ 2018 MHC 7496 in between Mohan V/s S.Nagarajan, CDJ 2018 APHC 970 in between V.Naga Vinay V/s Ch.Sambasiva Rao and another, CDJ 2015 MHC 8046 in between S.Balamani V/s Vijayashanthi, CDJ 2024 SC 665 in between Sri Dattatraya V/s Sharanappa, Crl.A.No.533/2015 in between H.V.Jagannatha V/s Prabhakar B.J, I have gone through those case laws. Negotiable Instruments Act provides for some presumption in favour of the complainant i.e., Section 118 reads as here: - "That every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration and that every such instrument when it has been accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred was accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration". Further Sec 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act provides for presumption in favour of a holder. It reads as here: - "It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque, of the nature referred to in sec 138, for the discharge, in whole or in part, or any debt or other liability." Combined reading of above said sections raises a presumption in favour of the holder of the cheque that he has received the same for discharge in whole or in part of any debt or other liability. However, it is settled principle of law that the presumption available u/s 139 NI Act can be rebutted by the accused by raising a probable defense.

The complainant has examined as PW.1 and he has reiterated the contents of complaint in his chief- examination. He has got marked Ex.P1 to P19. He has produced the cheques issued by accused and the same is marked as Ex.P-1 & 2, the signature of the accused is marked as Ex.P-1(a) & 2(a), copies of bank memos are marked as Ex.P-3 & P-4, copy of demand notice dated:20.04.2018 is marked as Ex.P-5, copy of postal receipt is marked as Ex.P-6, copy of returned notice is marked as Ex.P-7, postal cover is marked as Ex.P-8, postal receipt is marked as Ex.P-9, copy of postal acknowledgment is marked as Ex.P-10, copy of absolute sale deed is marked as Ex.P-11, copies of agreement of sale are marked as Ex.P-12 & P-13, Ex.P-14 & P-15 are the bank statements, bank memos are marked as Ex.P-16 & P17, copy of statement of account is marked as Ex.P-18 and copy of letter addressed to the bank is marked as Ex.P-19. He has been cross-examined by the counsel for the accused. Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026 Percontra, the accused has also stepped into witness box and orally deposed about his defense as stated supra and he has been cross-examined by the counsel for the complainant. Advocate for complainant has relied on the citations reported (2015) 8 SCC 378 in between T.Vasanthakumar V/s Vijayakumari, (2010) 11 SCC 441 in between Rangappa V/s Sri Mohan and (2007) 6 SCC 555 in between C.C.Alavi Haji V/s Palapetty Muhammed and another, I have gone through those case laws.

I have heard orally both side counsel and perused the written arguments filed by both side. Having regard to the pleadings and evidence placed on record it appears that acquaintance between the parties is not in dispute. At the outset the accused has admitted that both cheques at Ex.P1 and P2 belong to his account and he has duly signed on those cheques. Therefore, it is proved that cheques belongs to the account of the accused and they are issued in the name of the complainant. Therefore, initial presumption U/Sec.118 and 139 of NI Act has to be drawn in favour of the complainant as the Honorable Supreme Court of India in "Triyambak S Hegde v Sripad" (2022) 1 SCC 742 while relying upon the the constitution bench judgment of Basalingappa v Mudibasappa (2019) 5 SCC 418, under para 14 of its judgment reiterated that "once the cheque was issued and that the signatures are upon the cheque are accepted by the accused, the presumptions undee Sec 118 and 139 of the NI Act arise against the accused. That is, unless the contrary is proved, it shall be presumed that the cheques in question were drawn by the accused for a consideration and that the complainant had received the cheque in question in discharge of debt/liability from the accused." Therefore, as per Sec.118 and 139 of NI Act initial presumption has to drawn infavour of the complainant that cheque is issued in discharge of legally enforceable debt. The burden lies on the accused to rebut the said initial presumption on the scale of preponderance of probabilities.

In nutshell case of the complainant is that the accused has agreed to sell his property for total sale consideration of Rs.36,00,000/- and received Rs.30,00,000/- as advance consideration and executed sale agreements dated 07.05.2014 and 09.10.2015. But he failed to execute the sale deed and finally to refund the advance amount the accused has agreed to give Rs.45,86,000/- and issued cheques in discharge of the said liability, but those cheques dishonoured for the reason 'funds insufficient'. Hence this case. Even in his evidence, the complainant has reiterated the averments of the complaint. Though the counsel for the accused has much cross-examined PW.1 regarding his source of income, his occupation, his ITR documents, his land details and tried to dispute the financial capacity of PW.1, it is worth mentioning here that in the chief-examination of accused, he himself has admitted that through one Mr.Muniyappa, he met the complainant and borrowed Rs.10,00,000/- loan from complainant. Therefore, the series of questions asked by the counsel for the accused regarding financial capacity of the complainant holds no water, as accused himself has admitted the financial transaction with the complainant. However, as per the complainant, he has paid Rs.30,00,000/- Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026 towards advance sale consideration vide agreement of sale dated 07.05.2014 and 09.10.2015. Percontra, the accused contends that he never intended to sell his property, but he borrowed loan of Rs 10 lakhs from the complainant to which his signatures were taken in a blank stamp papers and bond papers for security purpose.

Firstly, the complainant has produced original sale deed dated 26.10.2007 at Ex.P11 which shows that title of the accused pertaining to the property intended to be sell. Ex.P12 is the sale agreement dated 07.05.2014, Ex.P-13 is the sale agreement dated 09.10.2015 executed by the accused in favour of the complainant. The accused admits his signature on Ex.P12 &P13 sale agreements, but he deposed in his cross-examination that his signature was taken in a blank sheets. It is pertinent to note here that the accused is the pygmy collector by profession, he deposed in his cross examination that he has complete knowledge about banking transaction. When such being the case, he being a prudent person of having worldly knowledge, this statement of the accused that he has singed to a blank e-stamp papers and bond papers, cheques appears to be vague and does not transpires the confidence of the Court. Nothing worth is elicited from the mouth of PW.1 to prove that he had taken blank e- stamp papers and bond papers, signed cheques from the accused for security purpose. Mere making suggestions to witness is not suffice. Therefore, there is no reason to suspect Ex.P12 & 13 sale agreements executed by the accused in favour of the complainant. On perusal of recitals of Ex.P12, at page No.2, it is crystal clear that accused has unequivocally admitted that he has received Rs.10,00,000/- by way of cheque and Rs.20,00,000/- by way of cheques & cash as per Ex.P13. ExP14 and 15 are bank account statement of the complainant which clearly shows that through cheque bearing No.413896 and 329275 Rs.20 lakhs has been transferred to accused.

During cross-examination in para No.3, the accused has admitted that he has received Rs.10,00,000/- by way of cheque from the complainant. Further he denied that as per Ex.P-13 he increased the sale consideration from Rs.11 laks to Rs.25 lakhs, He pleaded ignorance to the suggestion as per Ex.P15 and 14 account statement he received Rs.10 lakhs each. He denied the suggestion totally he received Rs.20 lakhs by way of cheques and Rs.10 lakhs by way of cash. If at all accused has not received 20 lakhs by way of cheque, he ought to have produced his account statements before the court to show his bonafide. He has produced only complaints filed by complainant against others. But not produced any admissible evidence to believe that he has not received amount of RS 20 lakhs by way cheques from the complainant. In AIR 2023 SC 5018 in between Rajesh Jain V/s Ajay Singh, Apex court held that " 31. Presumption, on the other hand, literally means "taking as true without examination or proof". In Kumar Exports v. Sharma Exports, this Court referred to presumption as "devices by use of which courts are enabled and entitled to pronounce on an issue notwithstanding that there is no evidence or insufficient evidence." Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026

As per above case law and in view of strong legal presumption given U/Sec.118 and 139 of NI Act the oral evidence of PW.1 corroborated with the documentary evidence at Ex.P12 & 13 I.e. sale agreements, and Exp14 and 15 account statements, the complainant has proved that he has paid Rs.30,00,000/- to the accused. Moreover, the accused has expressly admitted the financial capacity of PW.1 to advance a sum of Rs 10,00,000/-. In light of such admission, it is not open to the accused to dispute the financial capacity of PW.1 with respect to the remaining sum of Rs.20,00,000/-, as such, such contention is inconsistent and untenable. Sanjabij Tari vs Kishore S.Borcar, 2025 SCC Online SC 2069 Apex court held that "20. However, this Court is of the view that any breach of Section 269SS of the IT Act, 1961 is subject to a penalty only under Section 271D of the IT Act, 1961. Further neither Section 269SS nor 271D of the IT Act, 1961 state that any transaction in breach thereof will be illegal, invalid or statutorily void. Therefore, any violation of Section 269SS would not render the transaction unenforceable under Section 138 of the NI Act or rebut the presumptions under Sections 118 and 139 of the NI Act because such a person, assuming him/her to be the payee/holder in due course, is liable to be visited by a penalty only as prescribed. Consequently, the view that any transaction above Rs.20,000/- (Rupees Twenty Thousand) is illegal and void and therefore does not fall within the definition of 'legally enforceable debt' cannot be countenanced. Accordingly, the conclusion of law in P.C. Hari (supra) is set aside. ' Thus as per above case law, cash transaction is perse not illegal.

The only defense taken by the accused is that he has repaid entire loan to the complainant with interest. He disputes the extent of amount received. But irrespective of whether the amount in question is construed as refund of advance sale consideration or as repayment of a loan, the accused is legally bound to repay the sum received from the complainant. Although the accused has disputed the nature of the transaction, such dispute does not absolve him of his liability to return the admitted amount. In the cross-examination at para No.10 the accused has deposed that for Rs.30,00,000/-, he has paid 10% interest and it comes to Rs.3,00,000/-. He could not depose on which dates he has paid interest and principal amount to the complainant. But he told that he has paid it in presence of one Mr.Muniyappa. He deposed that he does not know exactly how much he has repaid so far to the complainant, but he has paid it in 2016-17 itself.

Therefore, except his self interested testimony, the accused has not produced any admissible evidence before the Court to prove that he has repaid principal with interest to the complainant. The accused has contended that at the request of the complainant, he has repaid the entire amount by way of cash and same appears to be vague, untenable and does not transpires the confidence of the Court. Admittedly, the accused is doing pigmy collection work having sufficient worldly knowledge about the loan transaction, banking transaction and also has complete knowledge about the potential consequences of issuance of blank signed stamp papers or bond papers and cheques. When such being the case, despite of having knowledge of issuance of blank signed cheques to the complainant, the accused contends that he has repaid entire interest and principal amount by way of cash without keeping any proof for payment appears highly improbable and raises serious suspicion. Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026 No prudent person would pay entire amount by way of cash without keeping any acknowledgment for having paid such huge amount. Admittedly Mr.Muniyappa is no more. Counsel for the accused has argued that in said murder case, complainant was one of the accused persons and he got enlarged on bail. Percontra, counsel for the complainant has argued that in the said case, some other persons have been convicted with life imprisonment and it is not related to the accused. However, both have not substantiated their arguments with cogent evidence. The questions as to whether Mr. Muniyappa died a natural death or was murdered, and if so, by whom, are wholly irrelevant to the dispute involved in the present case.

Even otherwise, the alleged involvement of the complainant in the said murder case, whether established or not, does not absolve the accused of his burden to prove the defence that he has repaid the entire amount to the complainant. Court cannot travel beyond the scope of this case. The accused must independently discharge the burden of proving repayment, and cannot rely on unrelated allegations to evade liability of cheques. No documentary evidence is produced to prove that the accused was possessing such amount to repay the same to the complainant at relevant point of time. Thus contention of repayment, lacks corroboration. In the cross-examination he has stated that he has repaid entire amount in 2016-17 itself. If that was the case, accused ought to have immediately taken steps to recover back the alleged security documents and cheques from the complainant. No such endeavor is made by the accused for the reasons best known to him. He has deposed in his cross-examination that the complainant has refused to return back his security documents and claimed higher rate of interest, subsequently he informed the same to Mr.Muniyappa also. Therefore, as per his own version in early 2017 itself the complainant become hostile to return back the security documents to him. Under such circumstances, any prudent person would have taken legal action against the complainant in anticipating of misuse of the documents or the cheques. He deposed that he has lodged a police complaint before CCB and he has given statement before the police. He has also deposed that police have told him that one Mr.Ravindra has already lodged complaint as per Ex. D6 and he can give statement in the said case.

Though DW1 couldn't identify his statement at ExD6 during cross examination, even such statement is given also, same will not exonerate the accused from repaying the amount to the complainant. If he is charging exorbitant interest, complainant shall face legal consequence as pe ExD6 and same is not a ground discharge the accused from this case. Admittedly both cheques are dishonoured for the reason 'funds insufficient'. Being vigilant person, accused could have given 'stop payment instructions' to his banker, even such efforts is also not made by the accused for the reasons best known to him. After cheques got dishonoured the complainant has issued legal notice as per Ex.P7 and same is returned with a shara 'door lock'. Though accused has contended that notice is not served on him, he has not disputed the address shown in the legal notice. Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026 Apex court in MMTC Ltd. and Another vs. Medchl Chemicals & Pharma (P) Ltd. and Another, (2002) 1 SCC 234 has specifically held that when a statutory notice is not replied, it has to be presumed that the cheque was issued towards the discharge of liability. It is held in 2006 CRI.L.J.1, in a case of Gorantala Venkateswara Rao. V/s. Kolla Veera Raghava Rao and another, that; "(B) Negotiable Instrument Act ( 26 of 1881), S.138 - Dishonour of cheque- Legally enforceable debt- Failure of accused in giving reply to legal notice issued by complainant- Is one of the strong circumstances to draw inference that accused borrowed amount from complainant and cheque was issued towards part payment of legally enforceable debt." In C.C. Alavi Haji vs Palapetty Muhammed & Anr (2007) 6 SCC 555, the Hon'ble Apex court has held; "

It is also to be borne in mind that the requirement of giving of notice is a clear departure from the rule of Criminal Law, where there is no stipulation of giving of a notice before filing a complaint. Any drawer who claims that he did not receive the notice sent by post, can, within 15 days of receipt of summons from the court in respect of the complaint under Sec 138 the Act, make payment of the cheque amount and submit to the Court that he had made payment within 15 days of receipt of summons (by receiving a copy of complaint with the summons) and, therefore, the complaint is liable to be rejected. A person who does not pay within 15 days of receipt of the summons from the Court along with the copy of the complaint under Sec 138 of the Act, cannot obviously contend that there was no proper service of notice as under Sec 138 , by ignoring statutory presumption to the contrary under Sec 27 of the G.C. Act and Sec 114 of the Evidence Act. In our view, any other interpretation of the proviso would defeat the very object of the legislation... " Therefore, defense of the accused that notice is not served holds no water as he has not deposited cheques amount before court as per law laid down by Apex court in aforementioned case law. The accused has not given reply to the notice and same is fatal to his defense. Therefore, it is evident that except oral say of accused, no credible, cogent, admissible evidence brought before the court to prove his defense that he has repaid entire amount to the complainant.

It is observed by the Court that for every question posed, the accused has given vague answers, stating that he was relying on Mr. Muniyappa and the repayment of the amount was made through him etc. It is further contended that Mr. Muniyappa had assured him that the documents would be retrieved from the complainant. However, However, in view of the fact that Mr. Muniyappa is no more, the possibility that the accused has taken such a stand only to avoid liability arising out of the cheques cannot be ruled out and it appears to be clear after thought. Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026 Though counsel for the accused has contended that there is no seal and signatures of the bank, on bank memos Ex.P3 & P4, by producing Ex.P16 and P17 bank memos as well as his account statement at Ex.P18, the complainant has clearly demonstrated that he has presented both the cheques to the bank and same is suffice to hold that the complainant has presented both the cheques to the bank. In most recent case regarding Sec 146 of NI Act, , Jagdish R vs Sri B S Ravi CRL.RP No. 1081 of 2018, Decided on 16 April, 2026, Hon'ble karanataka High court, held that "26. Therefore, the first contention on which the learned counsel for the revision petitioner has stated that there could not be any criminal prosecution for dishonor of the cheque, inasmuch as the bank memo did not contain proper endorsement of dishnour cannot be countenanced in law. Likewise, the contention that the seal and signature of the bank was a mandatory requirement when the cheque was sent for manual collection cannot also be accepted. In view of the electronic clearance, the seal and signature is not mandatory and therefore, seal and signature, official mark etc., on Ex.P.2 cannot be a ground to reject the complaint.

Since the complainant enjoys the presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, if at all the accused is of the opinion that bank endorsement vide Exhibit P-2 is incomplete or incorrect, he could have summoned his banker to establish that he had sufficient money in his account and the cheque was not presented to his banker at all for collection. Therefore, the ground that in view of Section 146 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, complaint is not maintainable, cannot also be countenanced in law. " As per above case law, merely because the seal and signatures are not appearing in the bank memos, which are produced initially, the entire case of the complainant cannot be brushed aside. The counsel for the accused has argued that after lapse of 3 years, from the date of sale agreement, the complaint is filed, this compliant, as it is not maintainable which is pertaining to time barred debt or liability and also relied upon the citations. I have gone through those case laws. It is significant to note here that as per the sale agreement, the accused has agreed to execute the sale deed within 12 months from the date of agreement of sale, which comes to an end on 09.10.2018. The complaint is filed on 05.06.2018. There is an initial presumption regarding date of issuance of the cheques as per Sec.118 of NI Act. Accordingly, Ex.P1 cheques have been issued on It is not proved that the cheques were issued in 2015 as alleged by the accused. Therefore issuance of cheques revives transaction in question, as such it is not construed as time barred debt or liability. Even otherwise within 2 years from the date of second agreement the complaint is filed.

In M/S M K Enterprises vs Kumari Varsha Pole, on 17 December, 2021 CRIMINAL REVISION PETITION NO. 375/20 Hon'ble Karnataka High Court, held Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026 that "26. Further, the defence that even if the version of the complainant was to be accepted as on date of presentation of the cheque, the debt was time barred does not defeat the rights of the complainant in the present factual matrix. The complainant has specifically asserted that the amount that was given to the accused was with the assurance that profits from the business would be given. The mere factum of payment stated to have been made in 2010 would not make it a time barred debt as on the date of issuance of cheque in 2018. As to when the debt occurred is a factual inquiry. The nature of the transaction was that in lieu of the investment made by the complainant, a hotel would be opened in the name of father of the complainant and profits from the business would be paid. Accordingly, when once a cheque is issued in light of the presumption of consideration by virtue of Section 139, it could be construed that a cheque has been issued towards a debt. As to whether the debt was time barred as on the date of presentation of cheque is to be proved by the accused. Even otherwise once a cheque is issued it could be construed to be a promise made in writing under Section 25(3) of the Indian Contract Act and if read in conjunction with illustration(e), the cheque could be construed to be valid and its dishonour actionable under Section 138 of NI Act. Accordingly, the contention that the cheque is issued as against a time barred debt and hence, unenforceable debt is liable to be rejected.

In K Hymavathi v. State of Andhra Pradesh and Anr, (2023) SCC OnLine SC 1128, the Supreme Court considered an appeal against the quashing of a complaint. It ruled that a promissory note executed to discharge a time-barred debt falls under Section 25(3) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, making it a valid and enforceable agreement. Sri Sudhakar Reddy C.B vs Smt Pushpa on 12 October, 2023 CRIMINAL REVISION PETITION NO.256/2022, Honb'le Karnataka High Court Held that Thus, when the questions formulated by the learned Single Judge of High Court of Bombay was referred to the Division Bench, it took pains in considering the matter from various facets and answered both the questions in the Affirmative. Thereby, holding that issuance of cheque is a promise in writing within the meaning of sub section (3) of Section 25 of the Contract Act and it is an exception to the general rule that the agreement without consideration is void. Thus, issuance of a cheque satisfies the ingredients of sub section (3) of Section 25, i.e., promise made in writing and signed by the person to be charged therewith to pay wholly or in part a dent of which the creditor might have enforced payment, but for the law for the limitation of suits and as such, the cheque becomes a cheque drawn towards discharge of a legally enforceable debt as contemplated by the explanation to Section 138 of the NI Act. Therefore, the position of law is laid down by the Division Bench of High Court of Bombay and there is no reason for not accepting the same. Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026

In view of the settled position of law, even if the contention of the learned counsel for the petitioner that the cheques were issued towards a time barred debt is to be accepted, by applying the above principle of law to the present case, issuance of cheques in question amount to written promise to pay the said debt, as provided under Section 25(3) of the Contract Act and it creates legally enforceable debt. Hence, it squarely attracts Section 138 of NI Act. As per above case laws, it cannot be construed that cheques are presented pertaining to time barred debt or liability, hence the compliant is absolutely maintainable. Instead of demonstrating that the full amount was repaid to the complainant, the accused is attempting to rely on hyper-technical grounds to evade liability under the cheque, which reflects his conduct before the Court. Further accused contends that complainant has filed various cheque bounce cases against different persons and also produced copies of those complaints before the Court and contends that he is money lender. Merely filing of multiple cheque bounce cases cannot be ground to hold that the complainant is money lender. No criminal action has been taken against him from the competent authority so far. Sec 24 of The Karnataka Money-Lenders Act, 1961, says that regarding Procedure of court in suits regarding loans.-- '(b) if the Court finds that the provisions of section 20 or section 21 have not been complied with by the money- lender, it may, if the plaintiff's claim is established, in whole or in part, disallow the whole or any portion of the interest found due as may seem reasonable to it in the circumstances of the case and may disallow costs.'

As per the said Act and the Rules framed thereunder, a money-lender is required to submit a report in the prescribed format to the prescribed authority. Non- compliance with this requirement constitutes a violation of the said provisions. However, such non-compliance does not, in any manner, affect the maintainability of a complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. By virtue of Section 24 of the Act, if the civil court finds that the provisions of Sections 20 and 21 have not been complied with by the money-lender, the court may disallow the whole or any portion of the interest found due. It is for the competent authority under the Act to initiate appropriate action against a money-lender who has violated the provisions of the Act. Therefore, the defence that the complainant is a habitual money-lender is not sustainable in law.

In S. Parameshwarappa S/O Late ... vs S. Choodappa S/O M.A. Shankarappa 2007(2)KARLJ19, Hon'ble High court of karnataka held that "Even in respect of the contention taken by the petitioners that it is a monetary transaction by way of money lending by the complainant and that he did not have the money lending license, the Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026 answer would be - this Court has already held in so far as a transaction of this nature, the question of the complainant having a money lending license with him does not arise. May be true that this Court in respect of the money lending as a matter of obligation on the part of the plaintiff in a suit for recovery of money, would insist, as a condition precedent, to have a money lending license. This is not a suit for recovery of money rather, the complainant is exercising the special powers provided under the NI Act for non-payment and dis-honour of cheque which is more in a quasi civil & criminal in nature. " Therefore, merely because the complainant has filed various cheque bounce cases against different persons, it will not exonerate the liability of the accused to establish his defense i.e. repayment of Rs. 30 lakh or issuance of cheques for security purpose. Therefore such contention of the accused holds no water. Further accused contends that he has not filled the details in the cheques. In view of Sec.20 of the NI Act the drawer of the cheque need not to fill entire details.

((2019) 4 SCC 197) ie Bir Singh V Mukesh Kumar, Apex court has held that "A meaningful reading of the provisions of the Negotiable Instruments Act including, in particular, Sections 20, 87 and 139, makes it amply clear that a person who signs a cheque and makes it over to the payee remains liable unless he adduces evidence to rebut the presumption that the cheque had been issued for payment of a debt or in discharge of a liability. It is immaterial that the cheque may have been filled in by any person other than the drawer, if the cheque is duly signed by the drawer. If the cheque is otherwise valid, the penal provisions of Section 138 would be attracted". Oriental Bank Of Commerce vs Prabodh Kumar Tewari , in (2024)12 SCC 165, Apex court held that '17. For such a determination, the fact that the details in the cheque have been filled up not by the drawer, but by some other person would be immaterial. The presumption which arises on the signing of the cheque cannot be rebutted merely by the report of a hand-writing expert. Even if the details in the cheque have not been filled up by drawer but by another person, this is not relevant to the defense whether cheque was issued towards payment of a debt or in discharge of a liability. ' Thus, in light of Section 20 of the Negotiable Instruments Act and the above-cited case laws, any inconsistencies in handwriting, pen, or ink on the cheques do not absolve the accused of liability, particularly when he has admitted the issuance of the cheques in favour of the complainant.

Therefore, having scrutinized entire evidence, this Court is of the view that accused has utterly failed to rebut the initial presumption given in favour of the complainant. Nothing worth is elicited from the mouth of PW.1 to suspect his case. Indeed by produced required amount of oral and documentary evidence, the complainant has proved his case beyond reasonable doubts. Further this court makes it clear that it cannot consider the some facts urged by the accused which are completely out of the scope of this summary proceeding case. With these observations court proceed to answer POINT NO.I IN THE AFFIRMATIVE. Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026 POINT NO.II:- In view of the reasons assigned in above point, it is ample clear that accused has committed the offence punishable u/s 138 of the Act. A bare reading of sec.138 of the NI Act indicates that the purport of sec.138 is to prevent and punish the dishonest drawers of cheques who evade their liability. The Hon'ble Apex Court in its recent decision in M/s. Meters & instrument Pvt Ltd. Vs. Kanchana Mehta reported in (2018)1 SCC-560 held at para 18(ii) that"(ii) The object of the provision being primarily compensatory, punitive element being mainly with the object of enforcing the compensatory element, compounding at the initial stage has to be encouraged but is not debarred at later stage subject to appropriate compensation as may be found." In view of the reasons assigned in above point, it is ample clear that accused has committed the offence punishable u/s 138 of the Act.

M/S Kalamani Tex vs P. Balasubramanian reported in AIRONLINE 2021 SC 82, Apex court reaffirmed aforementioned principle and held that "20. As regard to the claim of compensation raised on behalf of the respondent, we are conscious of the settled principles that the object of Chapter XVII of the NIA is not only punitive but also compensatory and restitutive. The provisions of NIA envision a single window for criminal liability for dishonour of cheque as well as civil liability for realisation of the cheque amount. It is also well settled that there needs to be a consistent approach towards awarding compensation and unless there exist special circumstances, the Courts should uniformly levy fine up to twice the cheque amount along with simple interest at the rate of 9% per annum."

The complainant himself has stated that he has given Rs.30,00,000/- to the accused whereas the accused admitted to refund the amount, as such this case if filed for Rs.45,86,000/-. Therefore, keeping in mind about above principles, having regard to the amount advanced, time from which it is lying with the accused and keeping in mind the primary object of the provision, this court is of the opinion that, rather than imposing punitive sentence, fine of Rs.65,86,000/- is imposed with a direction to compensate the complainant for her monitory loss, by awarding compensation U/Sec.357 of Cr.P.C, it would meet the ends of justice. Accordingly, this court proceeds to pass following ..... ORDER The accused is found guilty for the offence punishable U/s.138 of Negotiable Instruments Act. Hence, acting U/sec.255(2) of Cr.P.C, the accused is convicted and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs.65,86,000/- (Rupees Sixty Five Lakhs Eighty Six Thousand Only), in default of payment fine amount, he shall undergo simple imprisonment for 2 years for the offence punishable under section 138 of N.I.Act. Out of the fine amount collected from the accused, an amount of Rs.65,76,000/- (Rupees Sixty Five Lakhs Seventy Six Thousand only) shall be paid to the complainant as compensation U/s.357 of Cr.P.C. and the remaining fine of Rs.10,000/- shall be adjusted towards the cost of state expenses.
